clue.text: Old chap, love can be fun!

parts.note: 'old bean' is a dated British form of address for a man, so the chap is a bean
love is nil in tennis scoring, written as the round letter O

explanation.surface: A cheerful remark that an elderly man and a bit of romance can make for a good time.
explanation.walkthrough: BEANO is British slang for a lively party or spree.
explanation.definitionFit: A beano is a noisy celebration or spree, a bit of merriment.

clue.text: Shining light among the Broadway boys, but what a noise !

indicators.note: among says one piece sits in the middle of the group named by the other words

parts.note: The Bing Boys was a famous stage revue of the period, so the boys give the name Bing
a ray is a beam of shining light

explanation.surface: A star of the American musical stage turns out to make an awful racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shining light' looks like the definition, praise for a star; it is a beam, RAY, set inside BING from 'The Bing Boys', a hit revue of 1916.
explanation.definitionFit: Braying is the harsh loud cry of a donkey, a byword for an ugly noise.

clue.text: Brass on A1 may cause surface damage

indicators.note: may cause suggests the letters before it are made into something new by rearrangement

parts.note: the figure 1 is read as the letter I, giving A and I

explanation.surface: Polishing brass on a first-rate item could scratch its finish.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 means first-class, but here its 1 stands for the letter I; BRASS, ON and AI are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Abrasions are scrapes and scratches on the outer layer of skin or a material.

clue.text: Public figure in music

parts.note: something overt is done openly, in public view
one is a figure, a numeral

explanation.surface: A celebrity working in the music business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Public figure' reads as a celebrity; it splits into OVERT and ONE. 'In music' works like a dictionary label telling you the field of the term.
explanation.definitionFit: An overtone is a harmonic, a higher frequency sounding above the fundamental of a musical note.

clue.text: They are handy for fandango dancers

definitions.text: They are handy for fandango dancers

parts.words: They are handy for fandango dancers
parts.note: read as 'useful to have to hand' and also literally held in the hand, the clicking instruments Spanish dancers play

explanation.walkthrough: 'Handy' means convenient, and also worn in the hand: the fandango is a Spanish dance done to the click of these.
explanation.definitionFit: Castanets are pairs of wooden shells clicked in the hand to accompany Spanish dancing.

clue.text: "— opening on the foam Of perilous seas" (Keats)

definitions.text: "— opening on the foam Of perilous seas" (Keats)

parts.words: "— opening on the foam Of perilous seas" (Keats)
parts.note: a quotation with its missing word, from the 'Ode to a Nightingale' line about charm'd magic windows

explanation.walkthrough: The full line in Keats's 'Ode to a Nightingale' reads 'Charm'd magic casements, opening on the foam / Of perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn.'
explanation.definitionFit: Casements are hinged windows that open outwards, as the windows in the poem open onto the sea.

clue.text: Middlingly synonymous with "stint ""? Not much!

explanation.surface: A pedant notes that two words for being thrifty barely overlap in meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: As a verb the word means to give sparingly, a fair but not exact match for 'stint'; as an adjective it means barely enough.
explanation.definitionFit: To skimp is to stint, a near synonym, while as an adjective it means barely sufficient or meagre.

clue.text: Wherein' man has an angelic likeness; according to, Hamlet

definitions.text: Wherein' man has an angelic likeness; according to, Hamlet

parts.words: Wherein' man has an angelic likeness; according to, Hamlet
parts.note: points to Hamlet's speech praising man, where he is said to be like an angel in his deeds

explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet says of man: 'in form and moving how express and admirable! in action how like an angel!'
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet's speech man resembles an angel in his deeds and movement, the doing of things.

clue.text: The marksmen's shield from crazy Chloe

indicators.note: crazy says the name that follows is jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A girl gone mad snatches the trophy at a shooting contest.
explanation.walkthrough: The Elcho Shield is a long-running long-range rifle shooting match between the home nations of Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elcho Shield is the trophy contested by rifle teams from England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales.

clue.text: Was Haggard heroine in the liquor-shop ?

parts.note: She is the title heroine of H. Rider Haggard's novel 'She'
been is a past form of the verb 'to be', like was

explanation.surface: A question whether a gaunt female lead had visited the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haggard' looks like an adjective meaning gaunt; it is the novelist H. Rider Haggard, whose immortal heroine is called She.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebeen is an unlicensed Irish or Scottish drinking den selling liquor illegally.

clue.text: Tune diminuendo, not 'for the wind section, however

parts.note: an air is a melody or tune
a diminuendo is music played less and less loudly

explanation.surface: A melody fading away is no part for the brass and woodwind players.
explanation.walkthrough: The orchestral 'wind section' is the trap: the definition is about lacking wind, a still, stuffy place, which does no good to players who need breath.
explanation.definitionFit: Airless means without moving air or breeze, so no good for anyone needing wind.

clue.text: A case for diplomacy

parts.note: reads as a situation needing tact, but means both a document briefcase and an embassy official

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase sounds like a tricky situation needing tact; it names a slim briefcase, and also a junior embassy diplomat.
explanation.definitionFit: An attaché is an embassy official, and an attaché case is a flat briefcase for papers.

clue.text: Put in a bit extra

explanation.surface: Adding a little more to something.
explanation.definitionFit: To inset is to insert, and an inset is an additional piece set into a larger item, like a small map.

clue.text: Railway gremlin, beat type

explanation.surface: An underground train goblin with a regular rhythm.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is a pun: an underground railway (METRO) plus a gnome, said as NOME, a mischievous goblin.
explanation.definitionFit: The underground train sprite is a metro gnome, and the device musicians use ticks out a steady beat.

clue.text: Powdered hard fruit for Simians ?

parts.note: something powdered has been ground fine
nuts are fruits with hard shells

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes peanuts, the classic food tossed to monkeys at the zoo.
explanation.definitionFit: Groundnuts are peanuts, the traditional treat given to monkeys and apes.

clue.text: The geometer has a dotty way of showing it

definitions.text: The geometer has a dotty way of showing it

parts.words: The geometer has a dotty way of showing it
parts.note: dotty means eccentric but also made of dots: three dots in a triangle mark the conclusion of a proof

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dotty' means slightly mad, but the mathematicians' sign ∴ is literally three dots, used for the word that introduces a conclusion.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry proofs the three-dot sign ∴ stands for 'it follows that', 'hence', 'so'.

clue.text: I scan the image

parts.note: to con is an old verb meaning to study or scan closely

explanation.walkthrough: CON is an old word for studying or examining something carefully.
explanation.definitionFit: An icon is an image, especially a religious picture or representation.

clue.text: Sheriff's officer to apprehend the man from Warsaw

parts.note: to apprehend a person is to catch them
Warsaw is in Poland, so a man from there is a Pole

explanation.surface: A local law officer arrests a Polish visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: A catchpole was a medieval bailiff who arrested debtors.
explanation.definitionFit: A catchpole was a petty officer of justice, a bailiff making arrests for debt.

clue.text: Sent out for red light in the act

indicators.note: in says one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: a deed is an act
a ship shows a red light on its port side

explanation.surface: Someone was expelled for flashing a red light while being caught out.
explanation.walkthrough: A ship carries a red navigation lamp on its port (left) side, so the red light is PORT, put inside DEED.
explanation.definitionFit: Deported means expelled from a country, sent away by authority.

clue.text: " And, worst of all. I've Lalage " (Kipling)

definitions.text: " And, worst of all. I've Lalage " (Kipling)

parts.words: " And, worst of all. I've Lalage " (Kipling)
parts.note: a Kipling line with a word missing, in which the speaker laments no longer having his love Lalage

explanation.walkthrough: The missing word fills the gap before 'Lalage', the girl the speaker has parted from.
explanation.definitionFit: The speaker no longer has Lalage: she is gone, parted from him.

clue.text: Swiss fodder

explanation.definitionFit: Lucerne is a city and lake in Switzerland, and also the name for alfalfa, a crop grown as animal feed.

clue.text: Nightingales in the cinema ?

parts.note: Florence Nightingale was the lady with the lamp; cinema staff also carry lamps, their torches

explanation.walkthrough: Florence Nightingale was known as the lady with the lamp; the women who showed people to their seats in cinemas carried torches.
explanation.definitionFit: Usherettes were women who guided cinemagoers to their seats by torchlight.

clue.text: "1 have one of and goblins " (W. Tale)

definitions.text: "1 have one of and goblins " (W. Tale)

parts.words: "1 have one of and goblins " (W. Tale)
parts.note: a line from The Winter's Tale where young Mamillius offers a winter story of supernatural beings

explanation.walkthrough: Mamillius in Shakespeare's 'The Winter's Tale' says 'A sad tale's best for winter: I have one of sprites and goblins.' The page prints a blank before 'and goblins'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word names fairies or spirits, set beside goblins as tale-telling creatures.

clue.text: Distressing activity of Jaques mewling infant

definitions.text: Distressing activity of Jaques mewling infant

parts.words: Distressing activity of Jaques mewling infant
parts.note: points to the seven ages speech in As You Like It, where the baby is mewling and being sick

explanation.walkthrough: In 'As You Like It' Jaques describes the first age: 'the infant, mewling and puking in the nurse's arms'.
explanation.definitionFit: The baby in the speech is being sick, vomiting in the nurse's arms.

clue.text: In place of confinement you finally lose substance

indicators.note: finally places the following word at the end of the build

parts.note: a cell is where a prisoner is confined
U is a common short form of you, as in text speak

explanation.surface: Being locked up, you end up losing your very essence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' only says LOSE comes last; 'substance' is the definition in the chemical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Cellulose is the material forming plant cell walls, a chemical substance used for paper and fibres.

clue.text: A yarn from Old France

parts.note: yarn reads as a tall story, but is thread named after a French town under its old spelling

explanation.walkthrough: 'Yarn' sounds like a story; it is a fine cotton thread named after the French city Lille, formerly spelt this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Lisle is a smooth twisted cotton thread used for stockings, named from Lille's old name.

clue.text: Flaming head accompanied by tears

parts.note: head is old slang for this vegetable, flaming is a mild curse, and slicing it makes eyes water

explanation.walkthrough: In slang 'onion' means the head, as in 'off his onion'; and peeling one brings tears.
explanation.definitionFit: This bulb vegetable is slang for a head, and cutting it makes people cry.

clue.text: Whence came the quinquereme of Nineveh "

definitions.text: Whence came the quinquereme of Nineveh "

parts.words: Whence came the quinquereme of Nineveh "
parts.note: recalls the opening of Masefield's poem 'Cargoes', naming a distant biblical land of gold

explanation.walkthrough: Masefield's 'Cargoes' begins 'Quinquireme of Nineveh from distant Ophir'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the poem the ancient galley sails from this biblical land famed for gold.

clue.text: His magpie was noteworthy

parts.note: noteworthy means remarkable and also full of musical notes: the composer of the opera The Thieving Magpie

explanation.walkthrough: 'La gazza ladra' (The Thieving Magpie) is an opera by this Italian composer; 'noteworthy' puns on musical notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Gioachino Rossini composed the opera 'La gazza ladra', The Thieving Magpie.

clue.text: Mail for dispatch to distant station

explanation.surface: Letters being sent to a faraway post.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense reads the answer as two words: outgoing post.
explanation.definitionFit: Outgoing letters are out post, and a remote military or trading base is a frontier station.

clue.text: Coming-out in country style ?

parts.note: reads as a debutante's rural society debut, but means plainly a coming forth into view

explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming-out' suggests a debutante's launch into society; the answer is the plain act of coming out of somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Emergence is the act of coming forth or appearing from hiding.

clue.text: Trim garment

explanation.definitionFit: To dress is to trim or decorate, as in a shop window, and a frock is a woman's garment.
